--- title: "Fitting the Mean Field Before Kriging" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 execute: cache: false --- Kriging predicts a field as a mean field plus a GP anomaly. Where floats are sparse the anomaly reverts to zero and the map falls back on the mean field, so a mean field fitted to preferentially sampled profiles carries their bias into the gaps. This report compares three fits of the mean field on the toy jet of [the toy report](simex.qmd), each followed by the same kriging step. ## Toy with a seasonal cycle The field is the Bickley-jet OHC plus a seasonal cycle that is stronger in the north, $$ Z(x,y,t) = \underbrace{-\tanh(y/L) + a(y)\cos\!\big(2\pi(t-t_0)/365\big)}_{\mu(y,t)} \;+\; \eta(x,y,t), \qquad a(y) = 0.3\,\big\{1+\tfrac12\tanh(y/L)\big\}, $$ with $\eta$ the eddy part of the jet streamfunction. $\eta$ has zonal mean zero, so the box mean is $\bar Z(t) = \int Z(\cdot,t)\,d\mathbb P = 0.3\cos\{2\pi(t-t_0)/365\}$ exactly. The seasonal term is thermal only; the flow, including the weak drift toward warm water, is unchanged. Sixty floats are deployed uniformly on day $0$. After a one-year spin-up, $4$ years of $10$-day profiles give $146$ snapshots and $8{,}760$ profiles per replicate. In the example replicate below, 76% of profiles are in the warm southern half, and within a latitude band they also favour warm eddies: the anomaly $\eta$ averages \+0\.040 at the profiles against $0$ over the box. ::: {#cf35383c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_setup(ex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Z in the warm and cold seasons with that snapshot's floats, and the box mean through the record.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1205 height=414} ::: ::: ## Three mean fits All three fits use the same basis $h(y,t)$: a cubic in $u = y/250$ km, the annual harmonics, and the harmonics times $u$ (so the seasonal amplitude can vary with latitude). The cubic does not contain $\tanh$, so the mean is approximated, as in a real local window. The third fit adds $\log\hat q_t(x,y)$, where $\hat q$ is the stacked cloud density from anchors $4$ cycles back (as in the toy report), relative to uniform and floored at $0.05$. | fit | coefficients | intuition | |---|---|---| | OLS, no $\hat q$ | $\hat\beta = (H^\top H)^{-1}H^\top z$ | every profile is one vote | | GLS, no $\hat q$ | $\hat\beta = (H^\top K^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top K^{-1}z$ | correlated profiles share a vote | | GLS + $\log\hat q$ | as GLS, with $\log\hat q$ as an extra column of $H$ | crowded water is allowed to be warmer | $K$ is the anomaly covariance at the profiles: block diagonal by year (years as i.i.d. replicates), anisotropic exponential in $(x,y,t)$ with a $10^{-3}$ relative nugget. Its parameters are *oracle* values, the $e$-folding scales of the true $\eta$ ($\ell_x = 95$ km, $\ell_y = 210$ km, $\ell_t = 7$ d), so that only the mean-field step differs between fits. ::: {#e7548ddb .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_fits(ex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Example replicate. Left: zonal mean of each fitted mean field against the true mean field on one cold-season day. Middle: latitude distribution of all profiles (dashed: uniform). Right: box mean of each fitted mean field alone, against the truth.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1419 height=418} ::: ::: OLS lets the crowded south and its warm eddies dominate, and its mean field runs warm in both halves of the box, most of all in the sparse north. GLS treats a cluster of nearby profiles as fewer independent votes, which removes the warm offset in the south but leaves much of it in the north. The $\log\hat q$ column lets the fit attribute the extra warmth of crowded water to the crowding itself ($\hat\gamma = 0\.19$ here), so where $\hat q$ is typical or low the mean is not pulled warm. The $\hat q$ column also shifts the latitude coefficients, because $\hat q$ itself varies with latitude; $\hat\gamma$ is therefore not an interpretable effect, only part of a better prediction. ::: {#1810a5d6 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_q_term(ex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: expected float density q-hat on one day. Right: the true anomaly eta, with the contour where q-hat is twice uniform. Floats are expected where eta is warm.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1291 height=407} ::: ::: ## Three estimators of the box mean **Kriging.** Each fitted mean field is followed by simple kriging of the residuals, $$ \hat Z_{\mathrm{K}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \hat\mu(\cdot,t^*)\,d\mathbb P \;+\; \sum_i w_i\,\big\{Z_i - \hat\mu(x_i)\big\}, $$ with block-kriging weights $w_i$ from all profiles within $\pm 30$ d of $t^*$. The weights depend only on the profile positions and $K$, so they are the same for the three fits; only the residuals differ. **Cross-fit DR, leave one float out.** For each float $f$, the map $\hat m^{(-f)}$ is the mean fit plus kriging computed without any of float $f$'s profiles. In its GLS + $\log\hat q$ fit, the covariate comes from the other floats' clouds only. The pooled $\hat q$ at a time after $t^*$ is anchored partly on float $f$'s own positions near $t^*$, so using it would let float $f$'s realized position into the map that float $f$ checks. With $q_f$ the cloud density of float $f$ (expected profiles per km$^2$), $q = \sum_f q_f$ the stacked density, and $|\mathcal X|$ the box area, $$ \hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*) \;=\; \int \sum_{f}\frac{q_f}{q}\,\hat m^{(-f)}\,d\mathbb P \;+\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal X|}\sum_{f}\sum_{i\in f}\frac{Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)}{q(x_i)}\,\mathbf 1_{C}(x_i), $$ where $C = \{q\,|\mathcal X|/n \ge 0.05\}$ is the covered set. Off $C$ the $n$ maps are averaged with equal weight and no correction is made. The map term is not the full-data map. Each float's own influence on the map is removed in proportion to where that float was expected to be, which is what keeps a float from checking a map it helped build. Floats move independently given the flow. Conditional on the other floats, Campbell's theorem gives $\mathbb E\sum_{i\in f} g(x_i) = \int g\,q_f\,d\mu$, so if the clouds' density were exact, $$ \mathbb E\big[\hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}(t^*)\big] - \bar Z(t^*) \;=\; -\int_{C^c}\Big(Z - \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_f \mathbb E\,\hat m^{(-f)}\Big)\,d\mathbb P . $$ This is an exact identity, with a positivity remainder on the uncovered set only. With estimated densities $\hat q_f$ the bias picks up the product term $\sum_f\int (Z-\hat m^{(-f)})(q_f-\hat q_f)/\hat q\,d\mathbb P$. Under the correct cloud model, that error comes only from Monte Carlo and kernel smoothing in $\hat q_f$ ($200$ particles per cloud, $10$ km bandwidth) and from binning to the $5$ km grid. On average $C$ covers 99\.7% of the box. The DR step is applied to all three mean fits. Estimates are taken at every third snapshot of each of 30 replicates. The $60$ leave-one-out kriging maps share one cross-covariance per target. Each needs only the solve $K_{-f}^{-1}\,(Z-\hat\mu^{(-f)})$, so leave-one-float-out costs little more than a single map. ## One day, map by map The figures below follow the example replicate through one cold-season day (day 610) under the correct cloud model. All maps share the colour scale of $Z$, and all errors share one diverging scale. The box mean of each map is in its title. A single day shows how each estimator builds its answer, not how well it does on average; that is the next section. **Mean field.** Each fit's $\hat\mu(\cdot, t^*)$ next to the true $\mu$. OLS and GLS vary only with latitude, as their basis allows. The GLS + $\log\hat q$ fit also follows the $\hat q$ pattern, so it is warmer where floats are expected to gather. ::: {#7b092fc2 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_mean_maps(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top: the true mean field and the three fitted mean fields on one day. Bottom: their errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=1427 height=651} ::: ::: **Mean field + kriging.** Kriging adds the anomaly near the floats. Where floats are dense the three maps agree and follow the eddies. In the gaps they fall back to their own mean field, so the mean-field errors above survive there. ::: {#ee895903 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_krige_maps(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top: the true field with that day's floats, and the kriging map built on each mean field. Bottom: map errors, mapped and as a zonal mean by latitude.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=1427 height=651} ::: ::: **Cross-fit DR.** Top row: the map term, the mixture $\sum_f (q_f/q)\,\hat m^{(-f)}$ of the $60$ leave-one-float-out maps. Each float's own map is used where that float was expected to be, so the mixture is close to the kriging map but never lets a float check itself. Bottom row: each float's check $Z_i - \hat m^{(-f)}(x_i)$, coloured by the residual and sized by its weight $1/q$, over the faint error of the mixed map. Isolated floats far from the crowd get the largest weights: the northern floats are 33% of the floats on this day but carry 62% of the weight. The weighted sum of the checks is the correction added to the map term. ::: {#e795f3de .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_dr_maps(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top: weight of each float's check, and the mixed leave-one-out map for each mean fit. Bottom: map error by latitude, and each float's residual against its own leave-one-out map (size: weight).](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1436 height=651} ::: ::: ::: {#180c579a .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_day_summary(st)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box-mean estimate of every estimator on this day.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=986 height=495} ::: ::: ## Results under the correct cloud model ::: {#d54cd5c0 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} _show_fig(mf.plot_errors(df)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Error of the box-mean estimate over 30 replicates and about 49 target days each, correct cloud model.](meanfield_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=986 height=517} ::: ::: ::: {#bc018e68 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} HTML(fmt(mf.summary(dc))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

Under the correct cloud model the map hardly matters, because the correction is exact up to the error in $\hat q$. The price is variance. The DR sd (0\.030) is almost twice that of the GLS + $\log\hat q$ kriging map (0\.016), so per target day the kriging map has the lower RMSE (0\.018 against 0\.030). ``` ::: ::: With a wrong cloud model, DR is no longer unbiased. Its bias is then the product term: the map's residuals times the error in $\hat q$. The quality of the map starts to matter. - **Drift omitted, or noise too large.** The clouds no longer concentrate where floats actually gather, so the weights are too flat and the correction is too small. DR removes roughly a third to a half of the kriging bias. The $\log\hat q$ map is the best of the three in both cases (\+0\.0091 and \+0\.0126). - **Eddies displaced.** $\hat q$ is high in the wrong places, so the covariate carries almost no information ($\hat\gamma$ falls to 0\.032), and the three DR estimators end up similar (\+0\.0137 to \+0\.0153), still below the kriging maps. - **Noise too small.** This is the dangerous direction. Clouds that are too tight give floats landing in their thin tails very large weights, so DR over-corrects. On the OLS and GLS maps the bias becomes \-0\.0238, larger in size than the uncorrected kriging bias and of the opposite sign. On the $\log\hat q$ map, whose residuals are small, the over-correction shrinks to \-0\.0073. Coverage also drops to 95% on average. Across all five cloud models, the largest absolute bias of DR on the GLS + $\log\hat q$ map is 0\.0153, against 0\.0238 for DR on the OLS map and 0\.0206 for the GLS + $\log\hat q$ kriging map alone. A good map limits how much a wrong $\hat q$ can hurt. And since too little cloud noise costs more than too much, the noise should be calibrated, or erred on the wide side. **Not included here.** The covariance is oracle. An Argo-only version would estimate $K$ from the profiles, which preferential sampling also biases. That affects only the maps, not the validity argument for the DR step.
